Excellencies, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, it is an honor to be here before you on behalf of Belize and to join this important global conversation around a question that has become increasingly urgent for all of us with each passing year. The question of what truly makes a society resilient. We live in a time where uncertainty has often become almost certain. We witness conflict and displacement. We see widening inequalities, demographic changes, climate-driven shocks, rapid technological transformation, and growing concerns about the future of our children and our world. In these moments, resilience is often spoken about as though it were simply the ability to survive. But resilience is more than survival, and Ukraine and its people is an excellent example. Resilience is the ability to hold on to what makes us human while finding the courage and creativity to adapt to what is changing around us. The theme before us, World 2026, finding stability in times of uncertainty, reminds us that stability is not the absence of crisis. It is the presence of connection. It is knowing that when uncertainty arrives, our greatest strength is not that we are never tested, but that when we are, we will not face it alone. That is why for Belize, resilience is deeply rooted in something that is central to what we are as a people, our deep and enduring sense of community. Community for us does not simply mean to where we live, but how we live with one another. Belize is a very small country, yet we are a country of remarkable diversity. Our people come from different ethnicities, cultures, languages, traditions, and backgrounds. We are Creole, Mestizo, Maya, Garifuna, East Indian, Mennonite, Chinese, and many, many others. We speak different languages. We celebrate different traditions. We have different histories and stories. And still, we share one truth, that despite our differences, we understand that we need one another. When a family loses its home, neighbors come together. When a community is affected by a disaster, people share food, shelter, and whatever they have. When one person struggles, another person reaches out. And when our children need opportunities, we understand that their future is not theirs alone. It is a responsibility we all share. That is why for Belize, resilience is not simply about standing strong as individuals. It is about standing together as one people. Among them are the Maya, whose civilization and communities have demonstrated extraordinary continuity, adaptability, and strength across centuries. Today, Belize is honored to share a word from the Maya Yucatec Mestizo language that captures our our understanding of resilience. Muk'uyul. That was easy. Muk'uyul. This is our word, literally meaning the strength of his, her spirit or will, persevering through adversity. And behind this word is a much bigger story. It speaks to being determined, resolute, or persevering. It speaks to the capacity to endure, to adapt, to continue, to draw strength from those who came before us while creating a path for those who will follow. It reminds us that resilience is shaped by our ability to preserve our identity while adapting to change. Still, our experiences has taught us that societal resilience is not built only in the moment of a crisis. It was built long before the disaster arrived. It is built on our families, in our schools, in our communities. It is built when we teach our children empathy, responsibility, and respect. And it is built when institutions earn the trust of the people they serve. Again, that is why in Belize, we increasingly recognize that social development is not separate from national resilience. They are inseparable. A society cannot truly be resilient if families are struggling to survive. It cannot be resilient if women and girls live in fear of violence. It cannot be resilient if children are excluded from opportunities because of poverty or circumstance. It cannot be resilient if persons with disabilities are unable to fully participate in society. And it cannot be resilient if our most vulnerable citizens feel that their voices do not matter. Resilience, therefore, requires us to invest not only in infrastructure, but in people. It requires to strengthen social protection and access to opportunity. And above all, it requires us to protect the dignity of every individual. So once again, we add our voice to this global conversation with a word from our Yucatec Maya-Mesizo heritage,. May we continue to learn from one another. My country has lived through 53 days of road blockades. For nearly two months, roads closed, supplies were interrupted, and people who depended on a day's work did not know what the next day would bring. To understand those days, we must understand the difference between the anger people felt and what some political actors sought to do with it. Bolivians had reasons to be frustrated. Our country entered a period with a wounded economy, weakened institutions, and demands that had gone unanswered for years. People wanted change. They wanted to know when change would reach their homes. Those questions deserved answers. But some saw that anger as an opportunity. They took something deeply rooted in Bolivia, the courage of people to organize, protest, and demand to be heard, and tried to turn it into a way to destabilize a country that had just chosen a new direction. They wanted the old way of doing politics to return, a politics in which power is held through pressure, where roads are closed until a country gives in, and where a few can continue to live from a system that should serve everyone. I want to say plainly, the Bolivian people are not the blockade. The people are the market vendor who needs her goods to arrive, the farmer who needs to send a harvest, the driver stranded away from his family, the mother looking for fuel or medicine, the worker who wanted nothing more radical than the freedom to go to work. And the people also included those who protested in good faith, expecting their concerns to be heard, rather than used to prolong a political struggle. We defend the right to protest. A free people must always be able to challenge their government. But stopping food, work, production, and daily life does not give people a stronger voice. It makes them pay for someone else's attempt to take power. For 53 days, Bolivians paid that price. And for 53 days, they held on. They helped strangers strapped on the roads. They found ways to care for their families. They asked for answers without surrendering their hope that Bolivia could move forward. While some tried to make the country ungovernable, The people kept insisting that it was theirs to build. So when I look back on those 53 days, I do not ask which political side won. The people won. They held firm through an ordeal they did not choose. Their patience protected the possibility of a different future. Our response was dialogue. We kept the door open to demands. including questions left unresolved for 20 years. We brought people to the table and began the harder work of turning old grievances into plans and agreements. Dialogue did not mean accepting that the roads should stay closed. It meant refusing to let confrontation be the only way Bolivia knows how to solve a problem. We had to listen. We had to protect people's freedom to move, work, and live. This is why dialogue is our resilience. It gives a country the strength to face conflict without handing its future to those who profit from division. That strength has to be practiced every day. An agreement must be honored. A public institution must answer the citizen who comes to it. A worker must be able to earn a living. A producer must be able to produce. We are working to create a state that serves its people and makes room for their initiative. That work will be judged by what changes in Bolivia's lives. There will be more disagreements. There will be people in the streets, and there should be in a democracy. What matters is whether we can hear them, answer them, and keep the country open for everyone else at the same time. That is the choice before us each day. This idea that our resilience is strengthened by our connections to one another is not unique to the United Nations. It is deeply rooted in Canada's history and identity. Indigenous communities have understood for thousands of years that resilience is relational, rooted in community, responsibility, and a deep relationship with the land. That understanding is particularly important in a country such as ours, where geography brings both extraordinary strengths and unique vulnerabilities. We have the world's longest coastline, immense natural resources, and an Arctic that is warming more than twice as fast as the global average. Our changing climate is already testing our resilience through wildfires, floods, and extreme weather. In 2024, wildfires tore through Jasper, Alberta, destroying homes and disrupting thousands of lives. Canadians across the country stepped forward. They donated, they volunteered, they helped their neighbors. Governments worked together to support the community, and firefighters from around the world came to Canada's aid. That is resilience. It is not simply the ability to withstand a shock. It is the strength of the relationships that help us withstand it together. That is what we must continue to strengthen here at the United Nations, at home in Canada, and around the world. It is also the principle guiding my work as Canada's ocean envoy, where I'm bringing Canadians and international partners together to strengthen the resilience of our oceans and the communities that depend on them. Resilience is about relationships, their quality, their strength, their durability, and their diversity. Think about agriculture. A monoculture may be efficient, but it can also be fragile. One disease, one pest, one disruption can threaten the entire system. Diversity creates resilience. Canada is built on that principle. Diversity in our people, our regions, our industries, and our governments. Our federal system itself reflects the idea that different communities can bring different strengths to a common purpose. Excellencies, dear friends, a few years ago, I went to an exhibition in Estonia about the origins of our digital society. It tells the stories about people who had helped build up our digital public services, tech companies, and startup ecosystems. What struck me first, how many of them had the same starting point, the Digileap program. Tiger Leap was launched in 1996. Its aim was practical, to connect schools to the internet, to provide them with computers, to train teachers, and to give young people across the country the chance to develop digital skills. Today, That may sound like an obvious thing to do. But Estonia was then a young state, rebuilding its institutions after restoring its independence, with limited resources and many urgent priorities. We could not see what the digital future would bring. from social media and AI to cyberspace becoming a place of conflict. But we knew that investing in people's skills would pay off. A decade later, that investment proved its worth in a way no one had planned. In 2007, Estonia faced a large-scale cyber-attack targeting state institutions, banks, and media. By then, we already relied a lot on digital services. But we also had a society with good digital skills, experienced specialists, and strong cooperation between the public and private sectors. We had people who could understand what was happening and mobilize quickly. Because of those attacks, Estonia developed stronger cyber defense institutions and volunteer networks as well. For me, That is central lesson of Tiger Leap, that resilience is built up before a crisis hits. We often speak about resilience in terms of emergency plans, defense system, and the ability to recover after an attack. But resilience also grows much earlier in schools, in skills, in trust, and in the ability of people and institutions to adapt. Estonia is ready to share the experience it has gained in digital education, in teaching, training, in the use of AI in education, in cyber hygiene and digital resilience. Not because Estonia has a model that can simply be copied. Every country has its own needs and conditions. But we can share what has worked, what has not, and what we have learned from building up broad digital potential across our society. For Ukraine, I feel this conversation is especially relevant. Reconstruction is not only about rebuilding what has been lost. It is also about making choices whose full impact may only be seen years later. What skills should every child have? How do we prepare teachers for technologies that are still evolving? How do we build up digital systems that citizens trust and that remain resilient under pressure? These are questions that Estonia is ready to explore with you. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Madam Karis. Estonia truly leads by example in terms of digital resilience, and thank you for sharing your experience. And now I'd like to pass the floor to the First Lady of Lithuania, Mrs. Daina Nausodenien. Excellency, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Madam First Lady, for Lithuania's very unique experience and highlighting how will for freedom, bravery and creativity can overcome totalitarian and dictatorship regimes. And now I would like to pass the floor to the spouse of the Prime Minister of the Republic of Malta for her intervention. Madam, the floor is yours. Mrs. Lidia Abela.

Thank you. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. It is a great honour to co-host today's meeting, building on the vibrant and vital conversation that happened in Kyiv this August. And it is a particular pleasure to welcome First Lady Olena Zelenska here today. As we discuss resilience, "reziljenza" in Maltese, The resilience you and the Ukrainian people have shown in recent years is an inspiration to us all. Today's event is described as finding stability in times of uncertainty. Now, I don't know about you, but uncertainty strikes me as a bit of diplomatic understatement. It's certainly an understatement of how the world feels. People are anxious and looking for leadership. because they see a world where ever more powerful global forces are buffeting all our nations. Technology, climate change, the mass movement of people, culture wars. I could go on. Given that list, my message today might be a bit of a surprise, because I want to focus on why, despite all the challenges, I remain an optimist. I'm an optimist, not just about the future of my own country, but for all of us. Because I've seen the resilience that our citizens are capable of. And it continues to inspire me. It's a resilience rooted not just in the darkest days of Malta's history, the Second World War, or on the streets of Ukraine today, but in the small acts that our people take every day to adapt. to support one another and to find strength in the face of change so they can believe in their future. So what is our approach as a country? Malta believes that respect for human rights and the dignity of all is fundamental to building peaceful, inclusive and resilient societies. We know that no country, regardless of its size, can face today's challenges alone. For Malta, resilience has always been closely linked to our ability to adapt and to work with others. That's why we need a rules-based system and why institutions like the United Nations, the Commonwealth, and the European Union matter. Protecting human dignity, equality, and fundamental freedoms while ensuring that no one is left behind strengthens the trust and social cohesion upon which resilient societies depend. That means ensuring access to education and essential services, empowering women and young people, strengthening social protection, and building trust between citizens and institutions. We know conflicts and crisis disproportionately affect those already in vulnerable situations, including women and girls, children, persons with disabilities, older persons, displaced persons and minorities. It's why we must always ensure their full, equal and meaningful participation in decisions that affect their lives. Malta also believes in the accountability that comes from the voices of campaigners, human rights defenders and an independent media. An open, inclusive and vibrant civil society is essential in identifying emerging challenges, amplifying the voices of affected communities and thereby strengthening public trust in institutions. Resilience does not mean closing down, but opening up. I have faith that we can trust our citizens to respond in the right way if we put our faith in them. It was a former British Prime Minister, Harold Wilson, who said, "I'm an optimist, but an optimist who carries a raincoat." No question, there are plenty of storms around, and we have to be ready for the rain. But working together, we have enough umbrellas to go around. In conclusion, resilience is not simply about surviving a crisis. It is about being prepared before the crisis, supporting people through it, and ensuring that no one is left behind afterwards. Ultimately, resilience is about ensuring that even in uncertain times, people can continue to look to the future with confidence. Our circumstances may differ. Our aspirations are the same. Security, dignity, opportunity and hope. Malta is ready. I know. You are all ready. Together, let's build the resilient societies our citizens need and deserve. Thank you. Grazie, Hafna.

Thank you so much for sharing with us the Maltese resilienza and for highlighting how important it is to have the rule-based order and to protect human dignity and to safeguard equal participation in decision-making. Dear colleagues, we're a bit lagging behind time. I would like to ask you to be very short and crisp because we need to finish by 1 o'clock. And with this, I would like to pass the floor to the First Lady of Panama, Mrs. Maricel Coen de Molina, to present Panama's national concept of resilience. Thank you.

Good morning. Good morning, honorable Madam Olena Zelenska, First Lady of Ukraine and promoter of the Global Platform for First Ladies and Gentlemen. Dear First Ladies and Gentlemen, Excellencies, Ministers and Delegation, and my delegation from Panama, distinguished delegates, when I was asked what my country could add to this global language of resilience, I thought to myself, perhaps the best answer wasn't really by giving one definition. It was rather in the way we talk. Because language also tells the story of the people. Words that we repeat are stored in our experiences. Many times, the way we've learned, it is the way we've learned to face adversity. Panama, in Panama we say, sometimes you have to have thick skin, but maybe we also say, you have to resist thick skin. You have to face criticism, pressure, makes people making fun of you or difficult times without allowing this to paralyze us. But to have thick skin does not mean to stop, that you do not feel. It does not mean that you accept what's wrong. It doesn't mean that you have to harden your heart. We may have thick skin without losing awareness and sensitivity towards others and towards ourselves. After experience, after difficulty, another question arises that perhaps is more important. Panama now has found the answer. You have to move forward, keep on going. This means you look at the reality that perhaps we did not choose, but we ask ourselves, so what can I do now with what's happening to me? What can I do about it? And to ask ourselves that question may open up the way forward. And I see that all the time when I visit, when I visit all over Panama. I see a mother who loses a work, so she decides to learn a new trade so she can make money and help her children. I see that when somebody loses someone, but the next day they get up because there's a family that depends on them. When a family goes through difficulty in Panama, no one asks you whose problem this is. We all organize and help each other to face this problem together. That's how we understand that resilience is not only something individual. Resilience is also built together as a society. It's not enough to ask someone to be strong. we must also create opportunities for people to be able to pull themselves up again. If Panama could contribute an idea today there for this global vocabulary of resilience, then I would like it to be this. To be resilient is to allow ourselves to feel, to recognize our difficulties, but still be able to find the strength to move forward. Keep on going. Once we have hope again, when we believe once again in what we're capable of doing, and when we decide to give it our all, then we have another way of saying this in Panama. Let's put it all forward. Let's go for it. Thank you so much. Thick skin, move forward, let's all go with it.

Thank you, Jakson. That's the ACS experience. And now I'd like to pass the floor to the spouse of the Prime Minister of Slovenia, Mrs. Ushka Batzovnik-Jansha, to present Slovenia's national concept of resilience. Madam, the floor is yours.

Dear friends, dear Mrs. Zelenska, it's a great honor to be here with you today. I bring to you the experience of small country nestled between the southern slopes of the Alps and the northern shores of the Mediterranean. We have a very diverse landscape, which I believe is a gift of resilience. But our history also reminds us that peace and stability should never be taken for granted. In 1991, Slovenia experienced a war for independence. We were brave. prepared, reasonable, and importantly, well led. At that time, my husband was serving as Minister of Defense. Ukraine has all of these qualities today. And this is why Ukraine is succeeding. You were told that Ukraine would be completely taken over within 14 days. That did not happen, and it never will. In the first days of Russian aggression, my husband, at that time Prime Minister as well, traveled to Kyiv together with the Prime Minister of Poland and the President of the Czech Republic. By going there, we demonstrated our support and stood alongside the Ukrainian people, reinforcing their courage and determination. There is one key message that I would like to share in these difficult and uncertain times. Together, we are stronger. Friendship is essential to strength, and knowing that we are not alone gives us the courage to continue. In Slovenia, we have many voluntary and community organizations, which in times of peace and stability, primarily bring people together. strengthen connections and create a sense of belonging. But when difficult times come, these connections can become a powerful driving force for resilience and success. In Slovenia, this spirit is deeply rooted in our society. It is demonstrated by our strong voluntary organization of firefighters, of which I was a part of 20 years. voluntary blood donation, everybody who donates blood is entitled to a prize day of work, and volunteer mountain rescue service and many other volunteer organizations. Their message is clear, a sense of belonging to a community is a source of courage and resilience. We saw this during the COVID-19 pandemic as well. During these two years, I worked as a physician in the emergency department and in the intensive care unit. Those were extremely demanding and uncertain times. We entered the pandemic unprepared, as did many countries around the world. Yet, what helped us endure was the strong sense of solidarity among healthcare professionals and medical staff. and our shared commitment to one another and to our patients. We supported one another and we understood that in a crisis, no one can truly stand alone. This experience taught me something that goes far beyond healthcare. The sense of belonging and connection that we build with our communities in peaceful times is one of the most important investments we can make in resilience for difficult times. And last, a key word in the dictionary of resilience, I would add the word family and mother. I will tell you why. The deportation of forcible transfer of Ukrainian children and their enforced disappearance are crimes against humanity. We must stand together and fight for every child to be returned to his or her parents and family. Because every child belongs in the loving embrace of their family. No one should ever be allowed to take their right away. We must continue to speak loudly about this and raise public awareness. Dear Elena, you are proof that a strong woman and mother and united family can overcome everything, even in times of war. I believe peace will come soon. I wish you to remain strong till then and courageous. We will stand by your side. Thank you.

Thank you, Your Excellency, for a very emotional and beautiful speech, and also for highlighting the issue of abducted Ukrainian children by the Russian Federation, a grave breach of international law. We definitely need to return each and every child back home to Ukraine. And these are war crimes committed by Russia. With this, I would like to pass the floor to the First Lady of Romania, Mrs. Mirabela Gradinaru, to present Romania's National Concept of Resilience. Thank you.

Your Excellencies, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, Romania is honored to stand out today, once again, alongside Ukraine, bringing to the United Nations a conversation that began in Kyiv on August 24th. When we met in Kyiv last month, we brought with us words from different languages, histories, and cultures. words carrying the weight of what our societies have been through. Yet beyond the uniqueness of each national experience, we are speaking about something profoundly universal, something that holds a society together when certainty gives way to uncertainty. Out of that exchange came something rare in diplomacy, not a declaration, but a vocabulary. I would therefore like to thank Mrs. Olena Zelenska for bringing our different national experiences together into a shared global vocabulary of resilience. Romania contributed to that vocabulary with one word, "durzine." It means determination and courage, the strength to stand firm through hardship without losing our dignity, our values, our sense of responsibility towards others. For Romania's history has shaped this understanding of resilience and carried it across generation. We have learned that resilience is rarely one extraordinary act of courage. More often, it is the sum of 1,000 ordinary decisions not to give up. In Kyiv, We shared for the first time the meaning of Drzenje and the story behind it. Today, here at the United Nations, let me share that story with you once again to show where this idea comes from and where it lives today. Please turn your attention to the screen.

Before Drzenje became a word, it became a choice. Others are remembered by those they inspired. Derzhenya does not always carry a sword. Sometimes it simply refuses to stop searching. It walks one more mountain. It keeps one more promise. It returns home. Pressure changes. The instinct remains. Generation after generation, Romanians discovered that preserving who you are is sometimes the greatest act of courage. Today, the Resilient no longer belongs to history. It belongs to ordinary people, to those who keep building, keep caring, keep teaching, keep returning. People often think resilience means surviving one extraordinary moment, but we learned it also means surviving a thousand ordinary ones.

What you have just seen tells a Romanian story. It reminds us that standing firm is a choice we must make again and again. It is made by a teacher who keeps a village school alive, by a doctor who serves a small community, by a family that chooses to return home. This is the part of resilience that rarely makes into the press releases. Yet, it is precisely where the strength of a society begins. Resilience is the strength to withstand a crisis and the quiet resolve to remain true to yourself through the daily pressure of ordinary life. and its meaning reaches far beyond Romania. This is why this initiative matters. Madam Zelenska, you did not ask us simply to describe our histories. You asked us to name the instinct that helps our societies move through them. And as we listen to the experience of other countries here, something became clear, our words may be different, but much of what they describe is shared. The determination to protect what matters, the capacity to preserve dignity under pressure, the responsibility to stand by others, and the courage to continue. When we place those words next to one another, we begin to see something larger than any individual national experience seen. We begin to see the human architecture of resilience, And this is particularly important today in a world in which uncertainty is no longer exceptional. War, displacement, rapid technological change, and declining trust increasingly overlap. In such a world, resilience cannot mean simply becoming better at enduring crisis after crisis. Preparedness and resources are indeed crucial. But societies also depend on something more difficult to measure: trust, solidarity, and confidence that our values still matter when they become difficult to defend. Ukraine has demonstrated this with extraordinary courage. Every day, Ukrainians defend their homes, their freedom, their identity, and their future. Romania has stood with Ukraine from the beginning, welcoming Ukrainian families and children, supporting humanitarian efforts, and strengthening regional cooperation. And this experience has reminded us of a simple truth. Solidarity is not only what resilient societies receive. Solidarity is also what resilient societies give. No society has all the answers. and no nation wants the definition of resilience. But every society carries knowledge shaped by what it has survived, what it has protected, and what it has learned. Resilience may exist in different languages, but ultimately, it speaks to the same human instinct to protect what matters, to stand by one another, and to keep moving forward. Thank you.

Thank you, Madam, for sharing Romania's perception of resilience and for supporting Ukraine. And with this, I would like to pass the floor to the First Lady of the Turks and Caicos Islands, Mrs. Delthea Russell-Missick, to present the national concept of resilience. Thank you.

Distinguished First Ladies and gentlemen, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, there is an all African proverbs that many of us know. It takes a village to raise a child. I have always loved that proverbs because there is such a simple truth in those few words. None of us raises a child alone. None of us build a community alone. And certainly, none of us can build a nation or a more peaceful and stable world alone. We need one another. And perhaps in a world that has become so complicated, so fast moving, and at times so divided, we need to remind ourselves of that simple truth. We need one another. It seems especially fitting to reflect on that here in New York, one of the great meeting places of the world, a city surrounded by skyscrapers that speak to the human ambition, innovation, and progress. This city is shaped over generations by people who came from almost everywhere, from great cities and small villages, from large nations and tiny islands, They brought with them their cultures, their traditions, their hopes, and their dreams. And together, their stories helped to build this remarkable city. So even here, in one of the most modern cities in the world, there is something of the village around us. Because beneath the buildings, beneath the technology, and beneath the extraordinary achievements of human beings, A city is still built by people, by relationships, by trust, and by what people are able to accomplish together. When I think about our theme, World 26, finding stability in times of uncertainty, my thoughts keep running to those values of the village and to the lessons they may still hold for us today. I come from the Turks and Caicos Islands, a small chain of islands about 90 miles away from Miami, Florida, and just about three hours from New York. We are a chain of approximately 40 islands and keys of which eight are inhabited, surrounded by one of the largest barrier reefs in the world, and blessed with some of the most beautiful turquoise waters and powdery white sandy beaches on the planet. I may be a little biased in saying that, but I think I'm allowed to be. But those of us who live on those islands also understand something very well. Mother Nature can bless you, and it can also test you. The same waters that surround us with such extraordinary beauty can become part of a force that tests our resilience, our courage, and our fortitude. And in those moments, we are reminded that the strength of a country is not measured only by what it possesses or what it has built. It is also measured by the strength and character of its people. Life in many ways is much the same. It brings blessings, but it also brings moments that test us, some without warning, And in oftentimes, there are moments that we discover what truly holds us together. The Turks and Caicos Islands has had its share of those moments. In 2008, Hurricane Hannah and Ike struck our islands within days of each other. Then in 2017, we were tested again by Hurricanes Irma and Maria. And then, of course, COVID-19. came right after, a very different kind of storm, one that brought uncertainty to our homes, affected our livelihoods, and placed enormous pressure on our small island economy. Yet, in each of those moments, something very familiar happened. Our people came together. Neighbors checked on neighbors, families supported other families, Communities looked after the most vulnerable, and differences that may have seemed important before adversities suddenly mattered less. We adapted, we rebuilt, and we moved forward. And in many ways, we returned to the village. Whether it is a hurricane, a recession, a pandemic, the effects of climate change, or another natural or man-made crisis, In the final analysis, we find ourselves drawn on many of the same fundamentals. The strength of our families, the strength of our communities, our willingness to look out for one another, our ability to put differences aside when circumstances demanded it, and the trust that allows us to work together towards common purposes. Our experience in the Turks and Caicos Islands has shown us that these things matter. They have helped us through storms, through economic uncertainty, through global pandemics, and they have reminded us time and time again that resilience is not only about the strength of our infrastructure or the resources at our disposal. It is about the strength of the relationships between people. And perhaps that is one of the most important lessons of the village. Long before we spoke about resilience in the language we use today, our communities understood something very similar. When one person struggles, someone steps forward. When one family was in difficulty, others helped carry their burden. And when the community itself tested, people understood that they had a better chance of coming through it together than they ever would apart. That is why, even as our countries develop and our world become more technologically advanced, more interconnected, and more complex, I feel that we must not lose those fundamentals. We have to build on them. We have to adapt them to the realities of the world in which we now live. And perhaps most importantly, we have to extend the same sense of shared responsibility beyond the village, beyond our communities, and beyond our borders. As a First Lady, there is something that I have come to appreciate in a very personal way. It is a tremendous privilege, but it is also a demanding responsibility because it places you close enough to leadership to appreciate the weight of difficult decisions while at the same time giving you the privilege of meeting people whose lives are touched by those decisions. You hear their worries. You hear their hopes. And if you listen closely to those encounters, they will teach you something. They teach you humility. They teach you empathy. And they remind you that behind every policy, every international issue, there are human beings, people who simply want what all of us want, for People that we love, we want safety, we want dignity, opportunity and hope. I feel that particularly when I think about our children and the world we are preparing for them, whatever titles we carry, whatever positions we occupy, we must never become so removed from ordinary people that we can no longer hear them, see them, or understand what they are carrying. And when I think about that, it seems to me that the same is true of the relationships between nations. We have to be willing to listen to one another. to understand one another's experiences, and to recognize that there is something we can learn from each other, regardless of the size of the country we come from. The Turks and Caicos Islands is small, and we certainly do not pretend to have all the answers, but we have to learn from much larger countries and from one another. but we also have experiences, traditions, and perspectives that we can share. And that is the spirit in which I believe we must approach partnership, not as large nations and small nations occupying different worlds, but as countries that need one another, and that we can become stronger and more resilient by working together. Maya Angelou reminds us, "We are more alike, my friends, than we are unalike." And in a world where division can sometimes seem easier than dialogue, those words are worth remembering. That is why occasions such as this matter. They give us the opportunity not simply to speak about unity, but to practice it. by listening to one another, by learning from one another, and by asking a very important question, how can I help or how can we help each other build stronger communities and a more resilient nation? For me, and I would like to think for all of us, Defining stability and uncertainty is not about trying to create a world in which uncertainty no longer exists. Because history tells us that there is always going to be another storm, another challenge, another change that we cannot fully anticipate. So perhaps stability is not about eliminating uncertainty. Perhaps it is about strengthening our capacity to face it when it comes. And our experience has taught us that part of that capacity lies in the relationships we build before crisis, the trust we establish between people and institutions, and the partnership we develop between nations. Resilience is not something we should discover only after adversities arrive. It is something we should build every day. The old proverbs tells us, it takes a village to raise a child. Our world today may be larger, faster, and more complicated than the village that first gave us those words. But the principle remains, we still need one another. Perhaps our task now is to take the best of what the village has taught us, to strengthen it for the world in which we live today, and to do something even greater, to make the village larger. A village without borders, a village built on trust, a village built on partnership, a village built on compassion, a village where one of us If one of us is tested, we all stand together. Because ultimately, our greatest strength is not found in what separates us. It is found in what we can accomplish together. I thank you.

Thank you, Your Excellency, for a very powerful statement. Dear ladies and gentlemen, we need to conclude in two minutes, literally, because of the time limitation. And also, the President of Ukraine will speak at the UNGA. But we have a number of high dignitaries, participants from the floor. Let me just name them. Serbia, First Lady of Serbia, Honduras, First Lady of Honduras, United Arab Emirates, Secretary General of the General Women's Union, UNICEF, Global Director of Emergency Program, Costa Rica, Minister for Foreign Affairs, Liechtenstein, Her Excellency and we have one brief remark from the First Lady of Serbia, Mrs. Tamara Vucic. Please, the floor is yours. Thank you.

Thank you very much. Dear Olena, dear colleagues, First Ladies, dear friends. We have all agreed today that we live in the world of uncertainty and unpredictability. And we have agreed that the question is no longer whether we will face profound challenges, but how prepared and how strong we will be when they come. This is a kind of wrapping up today's event. To me, resilience means that even in times of crisis, a society remains exactly that, a society and a community. Social cohesion and national unity are therefore among the foundations of resilience. But unity does not mean uniformity or the absence of different opinions. Quite the opposite. Resilient societies return and turn diversity into strength, building upon what connects them, a shared identity and a sense of belonging. For centuries, gatherings, as we say in Serbia, sabori, have been an important part of the resilience of the Serbian people. In Kyiv, I spoke about Slava, a family gathering in honor of its patron saint, a tradition deeply rooted in our heritage. In a way, sabori are our largest Slavas, like gatherings and celebration of villages, towns, or even an entire country. One such gathering is the Vuk assembly or Vukov Sabor held since 1933 and regarded as the oldest cultural manifestation in Serbia.
